desc: This station involves a trauma primary survey with immediate management of a superficial neck wound over the external jugular vein, followed by a focused history, a nasal examination and counselling for a nasal septal haematoma.
explain:
Summary

This man has two life- or tissue-threatening problems hidden behind an apparently minor assault. The first is a superficial right neck wound over the external jugular vein, with an air entrainment risk. The second is a bilateral nasal septal haematoma that needs same-day drainage.

Primary survey (ABCDE)

Airway with cervical spine control comes first, then Breathing, Circulation (with haemorrhage control), Disability and Exposure. Call for help early and reassess after every intervention. Alcohol and a distracting injury mean the cervical spine cannot be cleared clinically, so in-line stabilisation continues.

External jugular vein laceration

The external jugular vein is covered by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, which holds a cut vein open. When the patient is upright, venous pressure at the neck is low or negative and inspiration can draw air into the circulation, causing venous air embolism. Features are sudden dyspnoea, chest tightness, hypoxia, hypotension and a mill-wheel murmur.

  • Immediately occlude the wound with direct finger or gauze pressure, then apply an occlusive dressing.

  • Lay the patient flat or head-down (Trendelenburg) with in-line stabilisation so that venous pressure at the neck is raised. Use head-down tilt with caution if there is a head injury.

  • If air embolism is suspected, a left lateral tilt may be used, but in a trauma patient it must be done as a log-roll with spinal precautions.

  • Get urgent senior help, give high-flow oxygen and consider CT angiography of the neck once stable.

Trauma deadly triad

Hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis each worsen the others and increase mortality. Prevent them by controlling haemorrhage, warming the patient actively (remove wet clothes, warm blankets, forced-air warmer, warmed fluids), limiting crystalloid and giving early balanced blood products through the massive transfusion protocol. Consider tranexamic acid within 3 hours if bleeding is significant. Follow lactate, base excess and coagulation results.

AMPLE

Allergies, Medications, Past medical history (and pregnancy where applicable), Last meal, and Events and environment. Here the allergy history is only useful if the reaction is clarified, because a remote non-severe rash is handled differently from anaphylaxis. Recent ibuprofen adds to bleeding risk, and alcohol and the last meal matter for any procedure.

Nasal septal haematoma

Blood collects between the septal cartilage and its perichondrium and cuts off the cartilage's blood supply. The presentation is nasal obstruction (often bilateral) after trauma with a smooth, red-purple, fluctuant septal swelling that does not shrink with decongestant. Untreated, it risks septal abscess, cartilage necrosis, saddle nose deformity and septal perforation. Treatment is urgent drainage as soon as it is diagnosed, usually with packing or splinting to prevent re-accumulation, plus antibiotics. Do not wait for swelling to settle.

Other management

  • Antibiotics follow eTG and local guidance, with the penicillin reaction type clarified.

  • Analgesia is paracetamol with titrated opioid, avoiding NSAIDs for now.

  • For a tetanus-prone wound with the last dose more than 5 years ago, give dTpa. Tetanus immunoglobulin is not needed with at least 3 documented doses.

  • Complete a secondary survey, imaging as indicated, ENT and surgical review, and factual documentation of the assault.
focus: Trauma primary survey in the ED: neck and nasal injuries
guide:
A high-performing candidate works in strict ABCDE order, recognises the neck wound as a possible external jugular vein injury and occludes it at once with pressure and an occlusive dressing. They position the patient flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation, and call for senior help early. They state hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis and take active steps to prevent them. They take a rapid AMPLE history, clarify the penicillin reaction, and examine the nose with a light, speculum and suction to identify a septal haematoma. They explain the risks (abscess, cartilage necrosis, saddle nose, perforation) and the need for same-day drainage, packing or splinting and antibiotics, and cover tetanus, imaging and secondary survey.

A borderline candidate leaves the patient sitting upright with the neck wound open, or does not explain why it is dangerous. They omit cervical spine control or warming, cannot name the deadly triad, or give a vague AMPLE history. They do not use a speculum, miss the septal haematoma or offer reassurance and discharge, and omit the tetanus, antibiotic and imaging plans.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Daniel Hartnett

  • Age: 32-years-old

  • Gender: Male

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No

  • Setting: Emergency Department resuscitation bay. You are anxious, a bit drunk and holding a wad of gauze to your nose.

Background (give only when asked, in short answers):

  • Events: About 45 minutes ago you were punched in the nose, then a bottle was smashed and swiped across the right side of your neck. You did not lose consciousness, you did not hit your head on the ground, and you remember everything. Your nose is blocked on both sides and throbs. The neck cut does not hurt much, but it was bleeding a lot.

  • Allergies: Penicillin. You had an itchy rash as a child and your mother told you not to take it. There was no swelling and no trouble breathing. Say this only if asked what the reaction was.

  • Medications: A salbutamol puffer when needed. You take ibuprofen occasionally for gym aches and took two tablets this morning. No blood thinners.

  • Past history: Mild asthma. You broke your nose playing football 10 years ago and had no surgery. No other operations. You had your childhood vaccinations, and your last tetanus needle was in Year 10 at school. You do not know whether you have had a booster since.

  • Last meal: A burger about 3 hours ago. You have had about 6 beers over the evening.

  • Social: You work as an electrician and are not on any other drugs.

Examiner findings (give as requested):

  • Airway: Speaking in full sentences with a normal voice. A small amount of blood-stained saliva in the mouth. No stridor, no neck swelling, no surgical emphysema, trachea midline. Mild midline neck tenderness cannot be cleared clinically because of alcohol and distracting injury, so in-line stabilisation or a collar is needed.

  • Breathing: RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, symmetrical air entry, resonant percussion, chest clear.

  • Circulation: HR 108/min, BP 114/72 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds, cool peripheries. A 3 cm laceration over the right sternocleidomastoid, oozing dark non-pulsatile blood. No expanding haematoma or bruit. A faint sucking noise is heard at the wound on inspiration when he is upright and the wound is open.

  • Disability: GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6), pupils equal and reactive at 3 mm, no focal deficit, BGL 5.6 mmol/L.

  • Exposure: Tympanic temperature 35.2°C. The shirt is soaked in blood and spilled drink. On log-roll with spinal precautions there are no other injuries and no spinous tenderness except the mild cervical tenderness above. If the candidate does not warm him, the temperature falls to 34.6°C.

Cue (examiner and patient): If the candidate leaves him sitting upright with the wound exposed or open for more than about 30 seconds, say: 'You hear a loud sucking and gurgling at the neck wound. The patient says he feels dizzy and has sudden chest tightness. SpO2 drops to 90% and BP to 92/58 mmHg.' If asked to auscultate the heart, report a churning (mill-wheel) murmur. If the candidate occludes the wound with pressure and an occlusive dressing and lays him flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation, the observations stay stable. If air embolism is suspected and the candidate suggests a left lateral tilt, accept it only if it is done as a log-roll with spinal precautions.

Nasal examination findings (when the candidate examines the nose):

  • The external nose is swollen and bruised, with slight deviation to the left. There is no active epistaxis and no clear rhinorrhoea (no halo sign on the gauze).

  • With a headlight, nasal speculum and suction to clear clots, both nasal cavities are obstructed by a smooth, red-purple, boggy swelling of the septum on each side.

  • It does not shrink with topical decongestant. A cotton bud palpation shows it is soft and fluctuant, not firm like a deviated septum.

  • The midface is stable, eye movements are full with no diplopia, and the teeth occlude normally.

Question to ask the candidate (once only, after the explanation): 'I just want to go home and sleep. Can this wait until the swelling goes down?' Accept a clear, empathic explanation that it needs treatment today. If the candidate uses jargon, say 'What does that mean?'
points: ABCDE: Airway (with cervical spine control), Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure. Work in order, treat as you go and call for help early.
AMPLE: Allergies, Medications, Past history (and pregnancy), Last meal, Events and environment. Clarify the allergy reaction type because it changes the antibiotic.
Trauma deadly triad: hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis. Prevent them with haemorrhage control, warming and early balanced blood products.

A superficial neck wound over the external jugular vein can entrain air because the investing fascia holds the cut vein open. Occlude it at once with pressure and an occlusive dressing, position flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation and get senior help.
In trauma, a left lateral tilt for suspected air embolism must be done as a log-roll with spinal precautions.
A septal haematoma risks septal abscess, cartilage necrosis, saddle nose and septal perforation. Treat with urgent drainage, packing or splinting, and antibiotics.

stem:
You are the emergency registrar. Mr Daniel Hartnett, a 32-year-old man, arrived by ambulance 15 minutes ago after being punched in the face and cut on the right side of the neck with a broken glass bottle during a fight outside a hotel. Paramedics report that their dressing came off during transfer. He is now sitting upright on the trolley with the neck wound exposed and a blood-stained shirt. A nurse is with you and can carry out any instructions you give. Monitoring is being attached.

The examiner will provide findings when you ask for or perform an assessment.
tasks: Perform (or describe) a primary survey (ABCDE), starting immediate management as you go, and state how you would prevent the trauma deadly triad (3 minutes).

Take a brief, focused AMPLE history from the patient, then examine the nose. The examiner will facilitate the nasal examination and give the findings. The nasal examination falls inside this 2-minute block (2 minutes).

Explain the nasal diagnosis, its risks and its treatment to the patient. Then outline to the examiner your further management plan, including antibiotics, analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, imaging and secondary survey (3 minutes).
